title: Building a Balanced Diet: Core Principles
content:
A balanced diet provides the nutrients your body needs to function correctly. Nutrients fall into two broad categories: macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, which provide energy) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals, which support specific functions).

Vegetables and fruits should make up roughly half of every meal, according to the USDA MyPlate guidance. Aim for variety and colour — different pigments in vegetables correspond to different protective phytochemicals. Dark leafy greens (spinach, kale), orange and red vegetables (bell peppers, carrots, sweet potatoes), and cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower) are especially nutrient-dense.

Whole grains (brown rice, whole wheat bread, oats, quinoa) should replace refined grains (white bread, white rice, most pastries) where possible. Whole grains retain their fibre, vitamins, and minerals; the refining process removes the bran and germ, stripping most of the nutritional value.

Protein sources should be varied. Lean meats, poultry, seafood, eggs, legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas), nuts, and seeds are all good options. Seafood twice per week is associated with reduced cardiovascular risk, partly due to omega-3 fatty acids.

Dairy or fortified non-dairy alternatives (soy milk, almond milk) provide calcium and vitamin D. Three servings per day are recommended for most adults.

Limit added sugars (found in sweets, sugary drinks, and many packaged foods), saturated and trans fats (found in fried foods, fatty meats, and many baked goods), and sodium (found in processed foods and restaurant meals). The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend keeping added sugars below 10 percent of total daily calories and sodium below 2,300 mg per day.

Ultra-processed foods — industrially manufactured products with many added ingredients including artificial flavours, colours, and preservatives — are associated in observational studies with poorer health outcomes and should be minimised in favour of whole or minimally processed foods.
source: Original — based on USDA Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020–2025 (federal publication, public domain) and MyPlate guidance
